goals: Tune C to trade margin width against errors
why: SVMs were the state of the art before deep learning, and remain strong for small to medium datasets with many features, such as text, bioinformatics and image descriptors.
explain: Many lines can separate two classes. An SVM picks the one with the **widest street** (margin) between them, like placing a road as far as possible from both villages.
Only the points on the edge of the street, the **support vectors**, define the boundary. Move any other point and nothing changes.

Real data overlaps, so the **soft margin** allows some violations. **C** controls the trade-off: large C means few violations and a narrow street (risk of overfitting); small C means a wider street that tolerates errors.
SVMs need **scaled features**. For non-linear boundaries, use the **kernel trick** (next topic).

example.title: Effect of C on a noisy dataset
steps: C = 0.01: wide margin, 12% training errors, CV accuracy 85%
C = 1: balanced margin, 6% training errors, CV accuracy 91%
C = 1,000: narrow margin bending around noise, 1% training errors, CV accuracy 84%
example.result: C = 1 wins. As always, choose by validation, not training error.

mistakes: Using it on millions of rows (training scales poorly).
takeaways: C trades margin width against training errors
use: Small to medium datasets with many features
avoid: When probabilities or interpretability are required

practice.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
for C in [0.01, 1, 100]:
    print(C, cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", C=C)), X, y, cv=5).mean().round(3))
